THE PROGRAM

HOW TO FIGHT

Move with the left pad. Tap up to jump, hold down to crouch.
P punch · K kick · S special · B block.
  • Direction changes every heavy. Forward + HP is an overhead that beats crouch-blocking; forward + HK lunges in; down + HP is a rising anti-air; down + HK sweeps. In the air, down + K is a dive kick.
  • Chain your buttons. A jab that connects cancels into another jab, a kick, a heavy, a special, a super or a throw. Heavies cancel into specials and supers. Whiff, and nothing cancels — you eat the recovery.
  • Crouching punches and kicks hit low. Blocking while crouched stops low attacks; standing block stops overheads.
  • Blocking still costs a sliver of health, so don't turtle all round.
  • Landing and taking hits fills the blue reel meter. At full, the SUPER button lights up.
  • Every fighter belongs to one of five classes, named on the select screen. Rushdown hits fastest and softest and folds quickest — Minnie, Tigger, Cinderella, the Green Lama. Heavy is the reverse: slow, enormous damage, deep health — Pooh, Thor, Black Terror, the Sailor. Zoners own the space in front of them, Technical fighters have an answer per angle, and All-Rounders sit dead centre — medium speed, medium attack, no holes.
  • A super is the one attack that reaches a knocked-down opponent — it sweeps them back off the floor. Normals and specials can't, and a super won't extend a combo that has already run long.
  • Specials always beat normals. Every fighter's special out-damages their hardest normal attack, and a super does at least five times your best normal — the hardest hit in the game, every time.
  • Firing a super stops the reel dead: the frame freezes, a title card burns in, and the camera pushes in for the hit. Every fighter's super looks different — Willie's floods the screen with ink blots, Pooh's turns it to sketch paper, Snow White's cuts to woodcut engraving, Stardust's to comic halftone, Mulan's is a single brush stroke, Thor calls lightning down, and The Owl kills the lights and leaves one searchlight.
  • Hitting someone during their wind-up is a COUNTER — 22% extra damage, called out on screen.
  • Two attacks landing on the same frame CLASH: both cancel, both fighters are thrown back, and you each bank meter. Take a long enough beating and you go DIZZY — stars, a wobble, and a free hit for them. Get knocked into the boards and you bounce off the wall.
  • In Arcade and Survival the reel can develop an omen — nitrate burn, hand-cranked speed, silent-era free blocking — announced before the round and tinting the picture.
  • Some later opponents show up as a Nitrate or Inkblot print: recoloured, marked with a ring under their feet, and considerably harder.
  • Win a bout and you get to splice the reel — pick one permanent upgrade from three, kept for the rest of the run.
  • Air kicks beat ground approaches. Anti-air specials beat air kicks.
  • T throws, and throws beat blocking outright — a turtling opponent is a free grab. Whiff one against a jump and you pay for it.
  • Hold back and press S for a second special. Every fighter has two, covering different angles: one for range, one for anti-air or closing in.
  • Double-tap left or right to dash. Back-dashes have invulnerable frames — the cleanest escape from pressure.
  • Tigger, Stardust and The Owl jump twice. Stardust, The Owl and Fantomah slow their fall if you hold up. Pooh, Thor, Black Terror and the Sailor shrug off one hit mid-heavy.
  • Keyboard: arrows or WASD, J punch, I heavy punch, K kick, O heavy kick, L special, N throw, Space block, U super.

PROVENANCE

WHY THIS IS LEGAL

Every fighter here comes from a work in the United States public domain, and every sprite is drawn from scratch in code — nothing is traced, copied, or ripped.
  • Willie & Minnie — the 1928 Steamboat Willie designs only: black pie-eyes, no red shorts, no gloves-and-yellow-shoes look. That later art is still Disney's.
  • Pooh & Tigger — E. H. Shepard's line drawings from Winnie-the-Pooh (1926) and The House at Pooh Corner (1928). No red shirt on Pooh; that's Disney's.
  • Snow White, Cinderella, Alice, Robin Hood, Pinocchio, Mulan — Grimm 1812, Perrault 1697, Carroll 1865, the English ballads, Collodi 1883, and the Ballad of Mulan. Centuries older than any film studio.
  • Thor — the Poetic and Prose Edda, 13th century. Red beard, iron gloves, no winged helmet nonsense. Marvel’s 1962 version is a separate creation and is not used here.
  • Stardust, Fantomah, Black Terror, Green Lama, The Clock, The Owl — Golden Age comics from Fox, Fiction House, Nedor, Prize, Comics Magazine Co. and Dell, 1936–1941, published by houses that folded without renewing copyright.
  • The Sailor — E. C. Segar’s 1929 Thimble Theatre strip, which entered the US public domain on 1 January 2025. The 1930s Fleischer cartoon version is still under copyright and is not used.
Two of the requests didn’t make it: Sandman (1939) and Dr. Mid-Nite (1941) are DC properties with renewed copyrights. The Clock and The Owl stand in — both older, both free. And one caution: copyright and trademark run on different clocks. A character can be free to draw and still be a live trademark, which limits how you brand and sell a release even when the art itself is fair game. Disney's later films adapted the same free sources. Adapting them yourself is the exact same right — you just can't borrow their version of the drawing. So this game doesn't.

Music: “Grand View” by SergePavkinMusic (menu) and a game theme by MiroStar (battle). Stage paintings are third-party artwork — check the licence before publishing.
